analysis.one_liner: Funds millions of affordable homes and down-payment grants for first-generation buyers, paid for by higher estate taxes.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2025 with 26 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was sent to four House committees and has not received a hearing, markup, or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would steer hundreds of billions of dollars over the next decade into building and preserving affordable housing, offer down-payment grants of up to 3.5% of a home's value to first-time, first-generation homebuyers, strengthen the rules that require banks to serve low- and moderate-income communities, and expand fair-housing protections. It pays for these programs largely by raising estate taxes on the largest inheritances and closing loopholes used to avoid them. It has sat in House committees since its introduction with no movement.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters facing high costs and displacement, first-time homebuyers whose parents do not own homes, residents of disinvested neighborhoods with depressed home values, public housing residents, tribal and rural households, and families facing housing discrimination (including based on source of income, sexual orientation, gender identity, or veteran status) would all gain if it passed. Nonprofit developers, community development financial institutions, and construction workers (through prevailing-wage requirements) also gain. The costs fall on the largest estates, big banks and nonbank mortgage lenders facing tighter Community Reinvestment Act obligations, and investors who buy foreclosed homes in bulk.

how_it_helps.text: Provides competitive grants to state, local, and tribal governments to remove zoning barriers to affordable housing — such as parking mandates, minimum lot sizes, and bans on multifamily building — with $2 billion authorized per year for fiscal years 2025 through 2029, and requires prevailing (Davis-Bacon) wages on funded construction.

Authorizes $48 billion per year for the Housing Trust Fund (which builds housing for the lowest-income households), $3 billion per year for the Capital Magnet Fund, a $70 billion public housing capital fund for fiscal year 2025, $2.5 billion for Indian housing, roughly $1.3 billion for rural housing programs in fiscal 2025, and a new $4 billion Middle Class Housing Emergency Fund — with funded units required to stay affordable to people below 120% of area median income in perpetuity.

Creates a down-payment assistance program giving first-time, first-generation homebuyers earning under 120% of area median income (140% in high-cost areas) a grant of up to 3.5% of a home's purchase price, funded for fiscal years 2025 through 2034, with buyers able to qualify by simple self-attestation.

Provides $5 billion in formula grants to help borrowers with negative equity pay down arrears, second mortgages, delinquent taxes, and repair backlogs in neighborhoods where home values are lower than rebuilding costs.

Strengthens the Community Reinvestment Act: regulators must assess whether banks actually meet the credit needs of low- and moderate-income communities, extends those obligations to nonbank mortgage lenders for the first time, and adds penalties for banks that repeatedly fail — including growth restrictions and clawbacks of executive compensation.
Expands the Fair Housing Act to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity, marital status, source of income, veteran status, or perceived membership in a protected class.

Restricts investor flipping of distressed homes: at least 75% of foreclosed FHA homes must be sold to owner-occupants or nonprofits, borrowers must get 90 days' notice and loss-mitigation review before their mortgage is sold, and at least 90% of foreclosed properties from sold loan pools must go to owner-occupants or 15-year affordable rentals rather than investors.

Grants states money to fund tenant protections — access to counsel in evictions, just-cause eviction rules, anti-harassment enforcement, and emergency rental assistance — as a condition of some housing grants.

analysis.who_pays: The largest estates would pay higher estate taxes — the bill raises rates, cuts the exemption, adds a surtax on high-income estates and trusts, and closes avoidance tools like short-term grantor trusts and valuation discounts. Banks and nonbank mortgage lenders would bear the cost of expanded Community Reinvestment Act examinations, community benefit plans, and penalties for failing grades. Investors who profit from buying foreclosed homes in bulk would lose a supply of cheap properties. If estate tax revenue falls short of the new spending, general taxpayers would bear the difference.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large estates, big banks, bulk home investors

drawbacks.text: The bill is enormously expensive — its authorizations run to roughly $100 billion or more per year in the early years (for example, $48 billion for the Housing Trust Fund and a one-time $70 billion public housing capital infusion) — and the estate tax increases that offset it are the bill's most contested element, raising the political bar to passage.

The estate tax changes — a higher rate, a smaller exemption, a surcharge on high-income estates, and new limits on trusts, valuation discounts, and conservation easement deductions — would fall on wealthy families and, critics argue, can complicate passing down family farms and small businesses, which is why the bill includes special valuation rules for certain farm and business real property.

Federal grant money is conditioned on local governments enacting zoning and land-use changes (by-right approval, density bonuses, parking reform), which critics view as the federal government overriding local control of land-use decisions.

Down-payment grants increase buyers' purchasing power, which can push prices up where housing supply is tight; the bill pairs the grants with large supply-side programs, but new construction takes years to reach the market, so near-term price pressure is a real cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and broadly distributed — lower housing costs, a shot at first-home ownership for families locked out of it, stronger tenant protections, and fair-housing coverage for groups the law still ignores. The costs are real but concentrated: the wealthiest estates and regulated financial institutions would pay, which is precisely the trade the bill is designed to make and precisely why it has no Republican support. The main honest criticism is scale and design risk: the spending authorizations are unusually large, the estate-tax offset would face intense opposition and political erosion, and demand-side aid could lift prices in the short run before the supply programs deliver. On balance, the bill does far more for ordinary people than it takes from them, but its ambition is also what makes it unlikely to pass as written.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2025 and referred to four House committees, but none has held a hearing or markup or brought it to the floor, so it is simply sitting.

narrative.text: Rep. Emanuel Cleaver introduced the bill on March 11, 2025, joined by 26 Democratic cosponsors including Reps. Ocasio-Cortez, Khanna, Nadler, McGovern, Pressley, Tlaib, and Omar; no Republican signed on.
The same day, the Speaker referred it to four committees — Financial Services, Judiciary, Veterans' Affairs, and Ways and Means — splitting jurisdiction and multiplying the hurdles it must clear.
On March 27, 2025, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity; no hearing, markup, or floor action has followed.

The Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill is not yet dead, but with Republicans controlling the House, the Senate, and the White House, and no bipartisan sponsorship, the main things standing between the bill and oblivion are time and committee inaction.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo holds: large banks and nonbank mortgage lenders face no new Community Reinvestment Act obligations, the largest estates pay no higher tax, and bulk buyers of foreclosed homes keep operating as before. Renters and would-be first-generation homebuyers gain nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large banks and wealthy estates, so far

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a Democrat (27 of 27 at introduction); there are no Republican cosponsors, and the Republican-controlled committees have not moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill raises estate tax rates, cuts the exemption, adds a surcharge on high-income estates and trusts, and closes avoidance tools like short-term GRATs, grantor-trust step-ups, and valuation discounts. This is the bill's main pay-for, and its cost falls entirely on the wealthiest households.

Community Reinvestment Act obligations are strengthened and extended to nonbank mortgage originators for the first time, with penalties for repeated failing grades — including growth restrictions and executive compensation clawbacks — and fossil-fuel-expansion financing is deducted from a bank's community-development credit.

industries.industry: Bulk buyers of foreclosed homes and single-family rental investors
industries.note: At least 75% of foreclosed FHA properties and 90% of foreclosed properties from sold loan pools must go to owner-occupants or long-term affordable rentals, borrowers get 90 days' notice and loss-mitigation review before loan sales, and contract-for-deed resale schemes are barred. These rules cut investors off from the cheap distressed inventory they profit from.

industries.industry: Nonprofit developers and community development financial institutions
industries.note: The Housing Trust Fund, Capital Magnet Fund, Middle Class Housing Emergency Fund, and community-partner purchase priorities channel tens of billions through nonprofit and mission-driven developers to build affordable housing.
Zoning reform grants and large construction funding increase building activity, with Davis-Bacon prevailing wages guaranteeing that federally funded construction pays union-scale wages.
Banks lose Community Reinvestment Act credit for loans that finance fossil fuel expansion, reducing the flow of bank capital to new fossil infrastructure.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding the House majority, the Senate, and the presidency, and with no Republican cosponsors, the bill is very unlikely to get a committee markup, let alone a floor vote, in this Congress. Its realistic paths are the ones familiar to prior versions of this same proposal: dying quietly at the end of the session, or having individual pieces (such as the down-payment grant or zoning grants) revived later as standalone bills. The March 27 subcommittee referral is the kind of step that precedes a hearing, but no hearing has been scheduled in the record.
